about: Retrieval answer key for `node tools/corpus/corpus.mjs eval`.
HOW IT WAS BUILT, AND WHY THAT MATTERS. The 15 questions and a first
answer key were written by the same session that then tuned retrieval
against them — a self-marking exam. So a second, fresh-context agent
derived its own key for the same 15 questions from ONLY the dossier and
coverage.md, with no access to the first key or the reasoning behind it.
Where the two disagreed, the disagreement is recorded in `reconciliation`
rather than silently resolved: a query whose correct answer two readers
cannot agree on is telling you something about the query, and about the
corpus, that a tidy consensus number would hide.
WHAT THAT SECOND PASS DID NOT FIX. It re-derived the ANSWER KEY, not the
QUESTIONS. The 15 questions are still the fixing session's own, chosen after
it had already seen which inputs broke — and four of them (2, 5, 6, 13) are
verbatim the crash/silent-zero repros from the PR that introduced this file.
Those four were guaranteed to score zero before the fix, so the headline
3/15 -> 15/15 is to that extent circular. The honest restatement is to drop
them: on the remaining 11 questions, none of which were selected for being
broken, the before/after is 3/11 -> 11/11. Quote that number if anyone
challenges the query set. Anyone adding queries here should add them BEFORE
making the change they intend to measure.
`primary`   — a system that misses all of these has failed the question.
`secondary` — legitimately relevant; credited, but not required.
`negative`  — plausible-looking distractors that should NOT rank highly.
SCORING (see eval.mjs): Recall@5 over `primary`, then MRR and nDCG at the
CLI's own retrieval depth — that is `--limit`, which defaults to 8, NOT 10.
nDCG uses gain 2 for primary and 1 for secondary. Scored on distinct SOURCE
ids in result order, not chunks. The depth deliberately follows the product:
evaluating deeper than `search` displays inflates nDCG for free.
STANDING CAVEAT: 15 questions over 52 sources is a smoke test. It
reliably detects 'broken' and 'clearly better'. It cannot resolve a
two-point nDCG difference, and no one should present it as if it could.
The primary safety gate is not the aggregate — it is that no query may
regress from found to not-found.

unretrievable_sources.12: AES TD1004 loudness — 404 at ingest. The document that actually states the numeric LUFS target is NOT in the corpus.
unretrievable_sources.52: ScienceDirect LLM-as-a-Judge survey — 403 bot-wall. The most on-point source for query 12 is absent.

queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree. Independent pass ranked 9 first (authoritative standards statement), 19 as the source that quantifies the drift, 48 as the real-world bug report.

queries.q: what loudness target for stitched segments
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT, and the first key was wrong. It listed source 12 (AES TD1004) as an expected hit; 12 404'd at ingest and has zero chunks, so it can never be retrieved. Worse, the independent pass argues the numeric target (-16 to -20 LUFS) may exist NOWHERE in the ingested corpus — 36 covers normalization workflow, not necessarily a number. This query is therefore partly ORPHANED, and that is exactly why it stays in the set: it is a test of whether a retriever admits it has nothing rather than confabulating coverage.

queries.q: does the server test cover embedded images
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT on ordering. First key led with 47 (Fordham Law Review); independent pass demoted it to secondary because it has only 1 chunk and is barely retrievable, and promoted 46 (Perfect 10 — the origin of the server test, literally about thumbnails). Independent view adopted. It also flags the question as ambiguous: the corpus's real thrust is whether the doctrine extends to AUDIO, which this phrasing does not ask.

queries.q: how do I fuse BM25 and vector results
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree on the pair; they differ on order. 29 is the canonical RRF paper but only 5 chunks; 30 is 15 chunks and lexically far closer to 'BM25 + vector'. Independent pass ranks 30 first on retrievability while conceding 29 is the more authoritative answer. Left unordered — both are primary.
Both keys agree. Coverage is thin (4 has 7 chunks); 20 matters only because WhisperX delegates diarization to pyannote.

queries.q: aligning word-level timestamps in long audio
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree. Independent pass contributed the `negative` list: Chromaprint (15, 22) matches 'align' strongly but means OFFSET realignment, not word alignment. Best distractor test in the set.

queries.q: where do I split a podcast into topics
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT — independent pass added 16 (Podcast Namespace chapters tag), which the first key missed entirely. Its argument: the question is ambiguous between 'which algorithm finds boundaries' and 'what boundaries already exist', and reusing published chapters is the cheapest real answer for a podcast while being invisible to semantic matching. Added as secondary; a good case for the founders that the corpus knows things the query author did not.

queries.q: cold start recommendations for new users
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree. Independent pass notes this is a discrimination test: 32 and 31 are cold-start for ITEMS (ads, promotions), same phrase, different problem. Ranking them above 8 would be a real miss.

queries.q: audio fingerprinting to detect a repeated ad
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT on whether the question is fair. Independent pass calls it poorly targeted: no source covers ad DETECTION, only fingerprinting for offset realignment, and the dossier itself flags Chromaprint's fit for spoken clips as unproven. Both primaries are 2-chunk sources. Kept, with the caveat recorded — a low score here is a fact about the corpus, not about the retriever.

queries.q: gapless playback of queued items on iOS
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree. Independent pass flags the risk that 33 (the literal bullseye) is a 1-chunk source and may lose to 13 (14 chunks) which answers a different question — composition, not queueing. Watch this one when comparing modes.

queries.q: what does TTS cost per character
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree on the trio. Independent pass adds a precision trap worth watching: 40 (ElevenLabs) has the most chunks but prices by subscription credits, NOT per character, so it will likely rank first while answering the question worst. 37 (TTS Arena) is quality-only and is marked negative.

queries.q: how do I stop an LLM judge from favouring long answers
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT with a caveat both keys accept. The best source (52, a taxonomy of judging biases) 403'd at ingest. Independent pass is explicitly UNCERTAIN whether 54 names verbosity/length bias specifically or only scoring bias generally, and notes the question asks for MITIGATION while the corpus mostly DOCUMENTS bias — which argues for promoting 51 and 53. Left as written, flagged as the second partly-orphaned query.

queries.q: can I republish someone's podcast audio
queries.reconciliation: DISAGREEMENT, and the first key was over-broad. It listed 10 (Hunley) as expected; the independent pass points out that every legal source except 50 is about linking/embedding WITHOUT hosting a copy — the opposite of republishing. 10, 46 and 11 were dropped from the key on that argument. 43 (Overcast's 1-minute cap) kept as practice-not-law.

queries.q: how are podcast downloads counted as a listen
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree. Independent pass flags a framing bug in the QUESTION: IAB counts downloads, not listens, and 18 is the source that makes exactly that point — so 18 matters more than its 2 chunks suggest.

queries.q: why did the clip-sharing apps die
queries.reconciliation: Both keys agree on sources; independent pass warns the corpus documents THAT they died, not WHY — the causal account lives in the dossier author's own TL;DR, not in any ingested source. Expect weak, inferential retrieval regardless of mode.
